subject: SnapFlow dedicated capacity request — pilot sizing & burst patterns
messages:
From: Alex Nguyen <alex@snapflow.ai>
To: Priyom Das <priyom@redwood.com>
Cc: Dana Li <dana.li@snapflow.ai>
Date: 2026-06-20T09:15:00-07:00
Subject: Pilot sizing for SnapFlow — burst behavior and pilot goals

Hi Priyom,

Thanks for taking this — we kicked off a new pilot project (SnapFlow Search Assist) and are evaluating dedicated capacity to meet our latency SLAs during bursts. High level: we expect a 3-month pilot that could convert to a reserved commitment if the numbers and reliability look good.

Quick context: SnapFlow is a realtime search/assistance layer for enterprise docs. Most traffic is read-heavy with short prompts (user query ~ 12 tokens) and model responses averaging 90–150 tokens. During product launches we’ve seen short spikes where concurrent sessions hit ~1,200 for a 5–7 minute window. Sustained baseline concurrency is ~120. Typical request mix: 70% single-turn queries, 30% multi-turn context (2–5 messages).

What we need from Redwood for the pilot:
- Sizing recommendation for a pilot pool that maintains p99 latency <= 300ms for short queries and <= 800ms for longer responses during bursts.
- Suggested GPU SKU(s) and occupancy targets. Our engineering org prefers we avoid large overcommit that causes p99 tail latencies to blow up.
- Expected token cost profile and where caching (prefix/KV) would deliver most value.

I attached a small telemetry sample (snapflow_telemetry_sample.csv) — it has a 72-hour snapshot with request timestamps, input tokens, output tokens, and a simple session id. Also attached is a short SLA doc.

Two clarifying points we can answer now:
1) Preferred region: us-west (GCP).
2) Security: SOC2 required; we’ll need Private with customer-managed keys if we proceed to commit.

Could we do a short sizing workshop? We’re available Tue/Wed afternoons PST.

Appreciate it —
Alex
VP Product, SnapFlow

Attachments: snapflow_telemetry_sample.csv (csv, 48KB), SLA_requirements.pdf (pdf, 12KB)
From: Priyom Das <priyom@redwood.com>
To: Alex Nguyen <alex@snapflow.ai>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-06-20T10:02:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Pilot sizing for SnapFlow — burst behavior and pilot goals

Alex — thanks for the summary and the telemetry snapshot, that’s perfect. I’ve looped in Karthik (solutions) and Marissa (sales lead) so we can pair on a quick pre-workshop sizing pass.

A few quick clarifying questions before the call so we can come with an initial hypothesis:
- Are the 1,200 concurrent sessions full-concurrency (i.e., every session actively generating at the same time) or a mix where many sessions are idle but hold KV cache?
- Do you rely on long context windows ( > 3k tokens) for multi-turn cases, or do you truncate/history select?
- Any constraints on GPU class (H100 vs A100) or preference to explore quantized variants to reduce footprint?

Proposed next steps:
1) We’ll prepare a pilot sizing sketch (GPU SKUs, nodes, occupancy targets, and expected token throughput).
2) Workshop (30–45m) to validate assumptions and walk telemetry.
3) Follow up with a short cost/commitment sketch and a suggested rollout plan (pilot -> reserved).

I can do Tue 6/22 2pm PST or Wed 6/23 3pm PST — which works best?

Cheers,
Priyom
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Folks — quick pre-call notes after scanning the telemetry:

Observations from the CSV: burst windows are very spiky (5–7 minute concentrated QPS), token distribution skewed (median input 10–14 tokens, 95th output ~220 tokens). That pattern suggests we should optimize for low-latency single-turn inference while enabling KV caching for multi-turns to reduce repeated context cost.

Initial hypothesis (pilot pool):
- Target SLOs: p95 latency <= 120ms for single-turn (short outputs), p99 <= 300–350ms during sustained baseline. For the 5–7 minute burst target, aim for p99 <= 800ms.
- GPU SKU: H100 80GB for the pilot if you need headroom on sequence length and KV cache; A100 80GB is possible if we use aggressive quantization and lower cache retention.
- Node count estimate (very rough): start with 3 H100 nodes with 8 concurrent generation slots each (occupancy conservative 60–70%), which maps to handling ~900–1,200 active short queries in a burst depending on batching efficiency.

Questions for Alex before the workshop:
1) What is the desired KV cache hit-rate target (if you have telemetry, even a rough estimate)?
2) Any hard p99 SLA penalties we should be aware of for pilot?
3) Are you open to exploring a hybrid approach: reserved capacity for baseline + burst routing to hosted pool? That buys headroom during spikes without immediate full-reservation costs.

I’ll draft a quick slide with assumptions and a simple token throughput table ahead of the call.

—Karthik
Lead Solutions Architect
From: Alex Nguyen <alex@snapflow.ai>
To: Priyom Das <priyom@redwood.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-06-20T13:45:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Pilot sizing for SnapFlow — answers and session_profile.json

Thanks — answers inline:
- Concurrency model: the 1,200 number is active generation concurrency during peak pushes (most sessions are active and generate at once for those 5–7 minute windows). Idle sessions are not the main driver in the peak.
- Context length: multi-turns rarely exceed 2,048 tokens; we truncate older history. So 2k windows is sufficient for our pilot.
- KV cache hit-rate: we don’t currently measure exact hit-rate; rough engineering estimate 40–55% for multi-turns in production traffic. We can instrument more if you need a better number.
- SLA penalties: none for pilot — we need to validate the model and reliability first.
- Hybrid approach: open to baseline reserved + hosted burst routing; that sounds attractive for cost control.

Attached session_profile.json has a small annotation of session lifetimes and a derived request-by-minute histogram. We can do Wed 6/23 3pm PST for the workshop.

Alex

Attachments: session_profile.json (json, 9KB)
